lessons.title: Study Session 1: Choosing Which Platform Metrics Actually Match Your Goal

blocks.text: Introduction Aichetou Kane, who raises her three children alone while leading reporting for a women's artisan cooperative's social media presence in Kaédi, reported the same two numbers, follower count and total likes, in every monthly update regardless of whether that month's actual objective was raising awareness of the cooperative or driving direct product orders. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about evaluating performance metrics for a social media presence. Distinguish a metric chosen for a specific stated goal from one tracked simply out of habit. Apply a method for matching a platform's available metrics to a specific objective. Recognise when a tracked metric no longer serves the goal it was originally chosen for. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 The Same Two Numbers, Regardless of the Goal Kaédi's women's artisan cooperative relies on Aichetou Kane to turn a month's worth of social media posts into a report the board can actually use, and that report always led with the same two figures, follower count and total likes, no matter what the cooperative's actual objective had been that month. A board member finally asked, during a review of a month aimed specifically at driving product orders, why the report said nothing at all about how many orders the cooperative's posts had actually generated. 2.2 What Research Found About Evaluating Social Media Metrics In 2019, the researcher Jan-Frederik Gräve published a study in Social Media plus Society examining which performance metrics actually mattered for evaluating a social media presence. His finding was that a metric's relevance depended entirely on how closely it matched the specific goal it was meant to serve, and that many accounts default to tracking whichever figures are most visible or easiest to find, follower counts and likes among them, regardless of whether those figures actually speak to the objective at hand. 2.3 Matching a Metric to an Actual Goal Naming the Specific Goal Before Choosing What to Track Deciding what a reporting period is actually meant to achieve, awareness, orders, enquiries, before choosing which metrics to feature, rather than defaulting to whichever numbers a platform surfaces most prominently, is the discipline Gräve's research points toward. Swapping Out a Metric When the Goal Changes Changing which metrics lead a report when the underlying goal for that period changes, rather than keeping the same figures out of habit regardless of what the account is actually trying to achieve, keeps a report connected to what it is meant to inform. 2.4 Key Practices Name the specific goal a reporting period is meant to serve before choosing which metrics to feature. Match each featured metric to the specific part of the goal it actually speaks to. Swap out a leading metric when the underlying goal for a period changes. Question a metric that has been reported the same way for months without anyone asking why. 2.5 A Worked Example: Aichetou's Goal-Matched Reports For the following month, Aichetou named the specific goal, driving product orders through the cooperative's online catalogue, before building the report, and led with click-throughs to the catalogue and completed orders, moving follower count and likes to a smaller supporting section. The board's questions that month focused directly on what had driven the strongest order conversions, a discussion the follower-count-led report had never once prompted. Nothing about the cooperative's follower count or likes was ever meaningless. Those figures were just never the ones that particular month's goal needed sitting at the top of the page. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Reporting the same headline metrics every period regardless of what that period was actually meant to achieve leaves a report technically accurate but practically disconnected from the decisions it is supposed to inform. Choosing a metric because a platform displays it prominently, rather than because it matches the current goal, tends to produce exactly this kind of habitual, disconnected reporting. 2.7 A Number Can Be Accurate and Still Miss the Point Every follower and every like the cooperative's account had ever earned was entirely genuine. None of it, however, told the board what a month built around driving orders actually needed to know, and only choosing metrics on purpose ever closed that gap. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to match a reported metric to a period's specific goal rather than tracking the same figures out of habit. Study Session 2 turns from choosing the right metric to actually pulling and organising the raw data behind it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a metric your own work reports regularly. Does it actually match the current goal, or is it reported out of habit? 2. Name a specific goal for one real reporting period and identify two metrics that actually match it. Practical Output: Practical Output A goal-matched metric selection for one real reporting period, naming the specific goal and at least two metrics chosen specifically because they speak to it. 7.0 References and Further Reading Gräve, J.F. (2019). What KPIs are key? Evaluating performance metrics for social media influencers. Social Media plus Society, 5, 1 to 9. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Philippians 3:14, on pressing on toward the goal to win the prize. Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:148, on each having a direction to turn to, so racing toward all that is good.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Pulling and Organising Data From a Platform's Own Analytics Tools

blocks.text: Introduction Deng Akol handles social media reporting for a youth sports league in Wau, and had spent a year taking a screenshot of each platform's summary dashboard at the end of every month, only to discover, when a coach asked how the league's engagement had changed since the season began, that nothing in the folder of screenshots could actually be compared to anything else in it. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about data literacy as an organisational competency. Distinguish organised, exportable data from a screenshot of a platform's summary dashboard. Apply a method for pulling and organising raw data from a platform's native analytics tool into a usable format. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Folder Full of Screenshots Deng Akol is responsible for turning a youth sports league's social media activity into a usable record in Wau, and had spent an entire season taking a screenshot of each platform's built-in summary dashboard at the end of every month, storing them in a folder as the league's record. When a coach asked how engagement had actually changed since the season began, Deng discovered the screenshots, each showing only a different platform's current snapshot in its own layout, could not actually be compared to one another or combined into any real trend. 2.2 What Research Found About Data Literacy In 2023, the researcher Guido Ongena published a study in Digital Business developing data literacy as a measurable organisational competency, based on a survey of 120 governmental agencies. His finding was that the practical ability to actually extract, organise and work with raw data, not merely view a summary presentation of it, was a distinct, learnable competency, and that organisations lacking it tended to accumulate exactly the kind of unusable, uncombinable records Deng's folder of screenshots represented. 2.3 Pulling Raw Data Instead of a Snapshot Exporting the Underlying Numbers, Not Just the Summary View Using a platform's export or download function to pull the actual underlying figures, rather than relying on whatever summary the dashboard happens to display, gives a report something that can actually be calculated with, compared, and combined across platforms. Organising Exported Data Into One Consistent Format Bringing exported data from different platforms into one consistent spreadsheet format, with matching columns and date ranges, is what makes a month-over-month comparison or a cross-platform total actually possible. 2.4 Key Practices Use a platform's export or download function to pull raw data, not only a screenshot of a summary view. Bring exported data from different platforms into one consistent spreadsheet format. Match column headings and date ranges across platforms before combining any figures. Save raw exports separately from the finished report, so the underlying numbers remain checkable. Re-export data on a consistent schedule rather than whenever it happens to be convenient. 2.5 A Worked Example: Deng's Organised Export Deng began exporting the raw engagement data from each platform's analytics tool at the end of every month, bringing the figures into a single spreadsheet with matching columns for date, platform, reach and engagement, and saving each month's export as a separate, dated file. Three months later, when the same coach asked about the season's engagement trend, Deng could show an actual month-over-month comparison across both platforms the league used, something the earlier screenshots had never made possible. The league's actual performance data had been sitting inside those platforms the entire season, waiting on nothing more than someone to pull it out in a form anyone could actually use. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Relying on a screenshot of a platform's summary dashboard, rather than exporting the underlying data, leaves a record that looks informative in the moment but cannot actually be compared, combined or recalculated later, which is the trap the league's season of screenshots fell straight into. Exporting data in whatever format each platform happens to offer, without bringing it into one consistent structure, creates the same practical dead end under a different name. 2.7 A Snapshot Answers Only the Question Asked That Day Deng's dashboard screenshots had never been inaccurate representations of what each platform showed at the time. A snapshot, however faithful, simply cannot answer a question about change over time, and only the raw data underneath it ever could. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to pull and organise raw data from a platform's own analytics tools rather than relying on dashboard screenshots. Study Session 3 turns from organising raw data to building a report structure the team can reuse period after period.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a record your own work keeps of past performance. Is it raw, exportable data, or a series of summary snapshots? 2. Export raw data from one real platform's analytics tool and organise it into a simple spreadsheet with consistent columns. Practical Output: Practical Output An organised spreadsheet of raw exported data from at least one real platform, with consistent columns for date, metric and value. 7.0 References and Further Reading Ongena, G. (2023). Data literacy for improving governmental performance: A competence-based approach and multidimensional operationalization. Digital Business, 3(1), 100050. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Numbers 1:2, on taking a census of the whole community by clans and families, listing every man by name. Qur'an, Surah Al-Kahf 18:49, on a record that leaves nothing small or great without enumerating it.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Building a Recurring Report Structure a Team Can Actually Reuse

blocks.text: Introduction Trinidad Nsue puts together the monthly social media figures for a chain of retail pharmacies in Bata, and built an entirely new report layout from scratch every month, choosing different section headings and a different order of figures each time, until a regional manager pointed out that no two months of the pharmacy chain's reports actually looked alike. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research established about diagnostic control systems used to monitor progress over time. Distinguish a recurring, reusable report structure from a document rebuilt from scratch each period. Apply a method for building a report template that stays usable across reporting periods. Recognise when a report template has stopped matching what the team actually needs to track. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A New Report, From Scratch, Every Single Month Trinidad Nsue is responsible for the monthly social media figures at a chain of retail pharmacies based in Bata, and had built a completely new report layout every month, choosing different section headings, a different order of figures, and sometimes an entirely different structure depending on what felt most relevant at the time. A regional manager reviewing several months of reports together pointed out that no two months actually looked alike, making it difficult to find the same figure twice in a row. 2.2 What Research Established About Diagnostic Control Systems In his 1995 book Levers of Control, published by Harvard Business School Press, the researcher Robert Simons described diagnostic control systems, recurring, structured reports used specifically to monitor progress toward a goal over time. Simons's central argument was that such a system's real value depended on its structure staying consistent from period to period, since a changing structure defeats the entire purpose of tracking progress, making it impossible for anyone to reliably locate the same figure or notice a genuine trend across reports. 2.3 Building a Structure That Survives Multiple Periods Fixing the Report's Sections Before Filling Them In Deciding on a fixed set of report sections, in a fixed order, before ever filling in a specific period's figures, gives a report a structure that stays recognisable and locatable from one period to the next. Updating the Template Deliberately, Not Casually Changing a report template only through a deliberate decision, reviewed and agreed before the next period begins, rather than adjusting it casually whenever a new idea occurs, keeps the structure stable enough to actually track progress against. 2.4 Key Practices Fix a report's sections and their order into a template before filling in any period's specific figures. Reuse the same template for every reporting period until a deliberate decision changes it. Review the template periodically for whether it still matches what the team actually needs to track. Change the template only through a deliberate, agreed decision, not a casual adjustment mid-cycle. 2.5 A Worked Example: Trinidad's Fixed Template Trinidad built a fixed template with four sections in a set order, goal for the period, headline metrics, month-over-month comparison, and next steps, and used the identical structure for the following three months, filling in only the specific figures and commentary each time. By the third month, the regional manager could locate a specific figure within seconds of opening the report and commented that comparing performance across months had become straightforward for the first time. Every individual month's figures had always been accurate in Trinidad's earlier reports. What had made them hard to use together was a structure that never held still long enough to actually be compared against itself. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Rebuilding a report's structure from scratch each period, even with entirely accurate figures inside it, makes it difficult for a reader to locate familiar information or notice a genuine trend across periods, a cost the pharmacy chain's reports paid every single month. Changing a template casually, without a deliberate decision behind it, produces the same instability under a different name. 2.7 Consistency Is What Lets a Reader Trust What They're Comparing None of Trinidad's earlier monthly reports had contained a single inaccurate figure. What they had lacked was a shape stable enough for a reader to trust that comparing one month's numbers to another's was actually comparing like with like. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to build a fixed, reusable report structure that stays consistent from one period to the next. Study Session 4 turns from a stable report structure to actually benchmarking one period's figures honestly against a prior one.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a recurring report your own work produces. Does it use the same structure each time, or does it change from period to period? 2. Sketch a fixed report template for one real reporting task, naming at least three sections in a set order. Practical Output: Practical Output A fixed report template for one real reporting task, naming a set order of sections that will be reused across future periods. 7.0 References and Further Reading Simons, R. (1995). Levers of Control: How Managers Use Innovative Control Systems to Drive Strategic Renewal. Boston: Harvard Business School Press. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Exodus 25:40, on making things according to the pattern shown. Qur'an, Surah An-Naml 27:88, on the work of Allah, who has perfected all things.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

A screenshot of a summary view cannot support the kind of comparison that raw, exportable data can

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Benchmarking Performance Against a Prior Period

blocks.text: Introduction Arlindo Trovoada, who compiles monthly figures for a tourism board's social media in Sao Tome, working remotely using a wheelchair-accessible home office setup, reported eight hundred engagements for the month with genuine pride, until a board member asked plainly whether eight hundred was actually good, a question Arlindo realised he had no honest way to answer. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what benchmarking research established about comparison as a basis for evaluation. Distinguish a benchmarked figure from a number reported in isolation. Apply a method for comparing a current reporting period against a prior one on the same terms. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Eight Hundred Engagements. Good or Bad? Arlindo Trovoada compiles the monthly figures for a tourism board's social media, based in Sao Tome and working remotely from an accessible home office, and reported eight hundred engagements for the month with genuine satisfaction at the figure. A board member asked plainly whether eight hundred represented good performance or poor performance, and Arlindo realised the report contained nothing that could actually answer that question, no prior month's figure, no target, nothing the number could be measured against. 2.2 What Benchmarking Research Established In his 1989 book Benchmarking, published by ASQC Quality Press, the researcher Robert Camp established structured comparison against a baseline as the actual foundation of meaningful performance evaluation, developed from his work reviving operations at Xerox. Camp's central argument was that a performance figure, on its own, carries no real evaluative meaning, and only becomes genuinely informative once it is compared against a clear baseline, whether a prior period, a target, or an external standard. 2.3 Comparing a Period Against What Came Before It Choosing a Consistent Baseline Period Selecting a specific prior period, the previous month, or the same month a year earlier, to serve as a consistent baseline gives a current figure something honest to be measured against, rather than standing alone. Comparing on the Same Terms as the Baseline Making sure a current period and its baseline are measured the same way, same platforms, same metric definitions, same date range length, keeps a comparison honest rather than misleadingly favourable or unfavourable. 2.4 Key Practices Choose a specific, consistent baseline period before reporting a current figure. Compare the current period against the baseline using the same platforms, metrics and date range length. Report the direction and size of the change, not only the current period's raw figure. Flag a comparison as unreliable if the baseline period was itself unusual for a known reason. 2.5 A Worked Example: Arlindo's Benchmarked Report For the following month, Arlindo reported the current engagement figure alongside the same month from the previous year and the immediately preceding month, using identical platforms and metric definitions for all three, and noted that the current month represented a genuine fifteen percent rise over the prior month, a real and meaningful improvement. The board's discussion that month moved directly to what had driven the fifteen percent rise, a conversation the earlier isolated figure had never been able to support. Eight hundred engagements was never, in itself, a meaningless figure to have reported. It only turned into useful information once something honest was finally placed next to it for comparison. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Reporting a current figure with no baseline to compare it against leaves an audience with no honest way to judge whether performance is actually good, the exact gap that left the tourism board's original report unanswerable. Comparing a current period against a baseline measured on different terms, different platforms or different metric definitions, produces a comparison that looks legitimate but is not. 2.7 A Number Alone Cannot Tell You Whether to Celebrate Eight hundred engagements said nothing on its own about whether the tourism board's month had actually gone well. Only once that figure had something honest and comparable standing next to it did the number finally start meaning something a board member could actually use. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to benchmark a reporting period against a consistent prior baseline rather than reporting a figure in isolation. Study Session 5 turns from honest comparison to telling a genuine change apart from ordinary statistical noise.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a figure your own work reports regularly. Is it ever compared against a consistent baseline, or reported in isolation? 2. Compare one real current metric against a consistent prior-period baseline, measured on the same terms. Practical Output: Practical Output A benchmarked comparison for one real metric, showing the current period alongside a consistent prior-period baseline measured on identical terms. 7.0 References and Further Reading Camp, R.C. (1989). Benchmarking: The Search for Industry Best Practices That Lead to Superior Performance. Milwaukee: ASQC Quality Press. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 2 Corinthians 10:12, on it not being wise to measure oneself only by oneself. Qur'an, Surah Az-Zumar 39:9, on whether those who know are equal to those who do not know.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Spotting a Misleading Spike or Dip Before You Report It

blocks.text: Introduction Zeinabou Illa assembles the monthly social media numbers for an agricultural cooperative in Zinder, and reported one week's sudden jump in engagement as proof that a particular post had struck a chord, only to watch the numbers settle straight back to their usual level the following week with no clear explanation for either the rise or the fall. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about misinterpreting random variation as a meaningful change. Distinguish a genuine shift in performance from ordinary statistical noise. Apply a method for checking whether an unusual data point reflects a real change. Recognise when a single period's spike or dip is being treated as a lasting trend. Avoid attributing a natural swing back toward average to a specific action that was taken. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Spike Everyone Wanted to Take Credit For Zeinabou Illa is responsible for an agricultural cooperative's social media reporting in Zinder, and one week's engagement figures jumped noticeably above the cooperative's usual range. Zeinabou reported it as evidence that a specific post, otherwise unremarkable in content, had struck a chord with the audience. The following week, engagement settled back to its ordinary level with no clear cause for either the rise or the return to normal. 2.2 What Research Found About Misreading Random Variation In 1973, the researchers Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published a study in Psychological Review examining how people form predictions from data. Among their findings was that people reliably misattribute regression to the mean, the ordinary statistical tendency for an unusually high or low figure to drift back toward the average on its own, to a specific cause, crediting an action for a rise, or blaming one for a fall, when the movement may simply reflect normal variation rather than anything that was actually done. 2.3 Checking Whether a Spike Reflects a Real Change Looking at the Point Within Its Normal Range, Not Alone Comparing an unusual figure against the account's ordinary range of variation over recent periods, rather than looking at the number in isolation, reveals whether it actually falls outside what normal fluctuation would produce. Waiting for a Second Data Point Before Calling It a Trend Treating a single unusual period as a possible trend rather than a confirmed one, and checking whether the pattern holds in the following period, keeps an isolated spike or dip from being reported as a lasting change before there is any real evidence it is one. 2.4 Key Practices Compare an unusual figure against the account's normal range of variation before reporting it as significant. Wait for a second period's data before calling a single spike or dip a trend. Ask whether a specific, identifiable cause actually explains an unusual figure before crediting one. Note when a figure has simply returned to its ordinary range, rather than treating the return itself as news. 2.5 A Worked Example: Zeinabou's Range Check After the spike settled back to normal, Zeinabou began tracking the cooperative's engagement figures over a rolling twelve-week range rather than period by period, and checked any new unusual figure against that range before reporting a cause for it. The next time engagement jumped noticeably, Zeinabou found it fell only slightly outside the normal range and waited a further week before reporting anything, during which the figure settled back on its own. The cooperative avoided crediting an unremarkable post with a success it likely had nothing to do with, and Zeinabou's reports began noting a figure's position within the normal range rather than reacting to every single new number. The original spike had never actually needed an explanation. It had simply been the kind of ordinary variation any account produces now and then, and only a longer view of the normal range ever made that visible. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Crediting or blaming a specific action for a single unusual figure, without checking it against the account's normal range of variation, reliably produces false explanations for what is often ordinary statistical noise, which is how the cooperative's spike earned credit it never actually deserved. Treating one period's unusual number as a confirmed trend, without waiting to see whether it holds, risks reporting a pattern that never actually existed. 2.7 Not Every Number That Moves Is Trying to Tell You Something The week's engagement spike had never carried a hidden lesson about what made a post succeed. Numbers move on their own some weeks for no traceable reason at all, and learning to recognise that was worth more than any explanation Zeinabou could have invented for it. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to check an unusual figure against a normal range before reporting a cause for it. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how a report's findings, now genuinely trustworthy, are actually presented to people who are not analysts themselves.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a recent unusual number in your own work. Was it checked against a normal range before being explained, or was a cause assumed immediately? 2. Track one real metric's normal range over several recent periods and note whether its most recent figure actually falls outside it. Practical Output: Practical Output A normal-range check for one real metric, showing several recent periods and whether the most recent figure genuinely falls outside typical variation. 7.0 References and Further Reading Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1973). On the psychology of prediction. Psychological Review, 80, 237 to 251. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: James 4:14, on not knowing what tomorrow holds, life being a mist that appears then vanishes. Qur'an, Surah Al-Hadid 57:22-23, on no disaster striking except it being written beforehand, so as not to despair or exult over what varies.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Presenting Findings to a Non-Specialist Audience

blocks.text: Introduction Prosper Mabiala writes up the monthly social media summary for a microfinance institution in Dolisie, and presented the board with a dense table of raw platform metrics and technical terminology at the monthly meeting, only to watch several board members leave the discussion without a clear sense of what, if anything, they were actually meant to decide. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about translating analytics knowledge for non-technical audiences. Distinguish a presentation built for a non-specialist stakeholder from one built for a fellow analyst. Apply a method for framing a report's findings around a decision the audience actually needs to make. Recognise when a presentation has drifted into technical detail the audience cannot use. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Room Full of Numbers, No One Sure What to Do With Them Prosper Mabiala is responsible for a microfinance institution's social media reporting in Dolisie, and presented the board with a dense table of raw platform metrics, reach, impressions, click-through rate, cost per engagement, at the monthly meeting, using the same terminology he would use with another analyst. Several board members left the discussion visibly unsure what decision, if any, the presentation had actually been asking them to make. 2.2 What Research Found About Translating Analytics for Non-Specialists In 2023, the researchers Ognjen Marjanovic, Greg Patmore and Nikola Balnave published a study in Information Systems Frontiers examining how analytics knowledge is actually transferred from technical experts to non-technical colleagues in multidisciplinary teams. Their finding was that presenting data to a non-specialist audience required deliberate translation, reframing findings around what the audience actually needed to understand and decide, rather than simply presenting the same technical material in a slightly simplified form. 2.3 Framing Findings Around a Decision Starting From the Decision, Not the Data Identifying the specific decision an audience actually needs to make, before choosing which findings to present, keeps a presentation anchored to something the audience can act on rather than a general tour of available metrics. Translating Technical Terms Into Plain Language Replacing platform-specific jargon with plain language describing what a figure actually means in practical terms is what turns a table of metrics into something a non-specialist audience can genuinely follow. 2.4 Key Practices Identify the specific decision the audience needs to make before choosing what to present. Translate technical terms into plain language describing what a figure actually means. Limit a presentation to the findings that actually bear on the decision at hand. Check, during or after the presentation, whether the audience can restate what they are being asked to decide. 2.5 A Worked Example: Prosper's Reframed Presentation For the following board meeting, Prosper identified the specific decision at hand, whether to shift budget from one platform to another, and built the presentation entirely around that question, translating reach and cost-per-engagement into a single plain comparison of which platform delivered more genuine interest per unit spent. The board reached a clear decision within the same meeting, something the earlier data-heavy presentation had never achieved. Not one figure in Prosper's original presentation had been wrong or beside the point. None of them, though, had ever been put into a form connected to the specific decision the board was actually there to make. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Presenting raw metrics and technical terminology to a non-specialist audience in the same form an analyst would use leaves the audience with accurate information they cannot actually act on, precisely the situation the microfinance institution's board found itself sitting in. Including every available finding, rather than only those bearing on the specific decision at hand, buries the point the audience actually needed under detail they did not. 2.7 Correct Data Still Needs a Translator Every figure in Prosper's original table had been calculated correctly. Accuracy alone had never been enough to make those figures useful to a board that needed, above all, to know what to actually decide. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to frame analytics findings around the specific decision a non-specialist audience needs to make. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Paid Social Advertising and Campaign Tracking, the next course in Pathway 49.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a data presentation you have given or received recently. Was it built around a decision the audience needed to make, or a general tour of available figures? 2. Reframe one real set of findings around a specific decision, translating at least two technical terms into plain language. Practical Output: Practical Output A stakeholder-ready presentation outline for one real set of findings, naming the specific decision at hand and translating at least two technical terms into plain language. 7.0 References and Further Reading Marjanovic, O., Patmore, G., & Balnave, N. (2023). Visual analytics: Transferring, translating and transforming knowledge from analytics experts to non-technical domain experts in multidisciplinary teams. Information Systems Frontiers, 25(4), 1571 to 1588. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Nehemiah 8:8, on reading clearly and giving the meaning so the people understood. Qur'an, Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:195, on a clear Arabic tongue.

quiz.q: A board member asked whether eight hundred engagements was good or bad, and Arlindo had no way to answer. What did this reveal?
options: The tourism board's social media strategy had failed
A figure reported without a baseline to compare it against carries no real evaluative meaning on its own
Tourism boards should not report engagement figures
Arlindo had miscounted the engagements
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Benchmarking Performance Against a Prior Period) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Camp's benchmarking research, what does a performance figure require to become genuinely informative?
options: A larger raw number than the previous period
Comparison against a clear baseline, such as a prior period or target
Approval from senior leadership before being reported
Nothing further; the raw figure is sufficient on its own
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Benchmarking Performance Against a Prior Period) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend when comparing a current period to a baseline?
options: Using whatever platforms and metrics are most convenient for each period
Measuring the current period and baseline on the same terms, platforms, metrics and date range
Comparing only against the single best-ever historical period
Avoiding any comparison to keep the report simple
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Benchmarking Performance Against a Prior Period) before continuing.

quiz.q: Engagement spiked one week and settled back to normal the next, with no clear cause for either. What did this reveal?
options: The post responsible had been deliberately promoted
An unusual figure can reflect ordinary statistical variation rather than a specific, identifiable cause
Agricultural cooperatives should not track engagement
The cooperative's account had been compromised
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Spotting a Misleading Spike or Dip Before You Report It) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Kahneman and Tversky's 1973 research, what do people reliably misattribute?
options: Genuine trends to random chance
Regression to the mean, ordinary statistical variation, to a specific cause
Accurate data to measurement error
Long-term patterns to short-term noise
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Spotting a Misleading Spike or Dip Before You Report It) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend before reporting a cause for an unusual figure?
options: Immediately crediting the most recent action taken
Comparing the figure against the account's normal range of variation
Assuming every unusual figure reflects a genuine change
Reporting the figure without any further review
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Spotting a Misleading Spike or Dip Before You Report It) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Aichetou's report always led with follower count and likes, even during a month focused on driving orders. What did this reveal?

Tracking the same metrics regardless of the current goal leaves a report disconnected from the decisions it should inform
Artisan cooperatives should not use social media for reporting
The board had misunderstood the report's contents

finalQuiz.q: According to Gräve's 2019 research, what determines a metric's actual relevance?

How closely the metric matches the specific goal it is meant to serve
The total size of the account's following
Whether the metric has been tracked historically
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Choosing Which Platform Metrics Actually Match Your Goal) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend doing before choosing which metrics to feature in a report?
options: Featuring whichever metrics the platform displays most prominently
Naming the specific goal the reporting period is meant to serve
Reporting every available metric to ensure completeness
Copying the previous period's metric selection unchanged
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Choosing Which Platform Metrics Actually Match Your Goal) before continuing.
